stemMd:
Two rules apply at a riverside lido.

- The lido opens only if a lifeguard is on duty.
- A lifeguard is never on duty during a thunderstorm.

Which one of the following conclusions follows with certainty?

options.label: A
options.textMd: If there is a thunderstorm, the lido does not open.

options.label: B
options.textMd: If the lido does not open, there is a thunderstorm.

options.label: C
options.textMd: If no lifeguard is on duty, there is a thunderstorm.

options.label: D
options.textMd: If there is no thunderstorm, the lido opens.

options.label: E
options.textMd: If a lifeguard is on duty, the lido opens.

explanationMd:
Translate the rules into "if ... then". "The lido opens only if a lifeguard is on duty" means: open leads to lifeguard on duty. "A lifeguard is never on duty during a thunderstorm" means: storm leads to no lifeguard.

Chain them. A storm means no lifeguard. The contrapositive of the first rule says no lifeguard means the lido is not open. So a storm means the lido does not open. That is the choice that follows with certainty.

The others each turn a conditional around or deny its front half. "Only if" gives a necessary condition, not a sufficient one, which rules out the choice saying a lifeguard on duty makes the lido open. Reversing a valid conclusion (closed leads to storm) or reversing a premise (no lifeguard leads to storm) changes its meaning. Denying the front (no storm, so the lido opens) ignores that a lifeguard can be missing for some other reason.

**Check:** for any doubtful choice, invent an ordinary day that satisfies both rules and breaks the choice. A calm day on which the lifeguard is ill, so the lido stays shut, breaks three of the wrong choices at once.

distractorRationale.d: This denies the antecedent of the chained conclusion (a storm means the lido stays shut) and treats the absence of a storm as enough to open. A day with no storm can still have no lifeguard, and then the first rule keeps the lido shut.
distractorRationale.b: This reverses the conclusion just derived. The lido can stay closed for reasons other than a storm, such as a lifeguard simply not turning up.
distractorRationale.e: This turns "only if" around. A lifeguard on duty is necessary for opening, not sufficient; the lido may still stay closed.
distractorRationale.c: This reverses the second rule. Storms rule out a lifeguard, but a lifeguard can be absent on a calm day too.

accessibilityText: A logic question about two rules for a riverside lido: it opens only if a lifeguard is on duty, and a lifeguard is never on duty during a thunderstorm. The question asks which of five if-then conclusions follows with certainty. No notation or figures.

independentSolve.workingNotes: 'Opens only if lifeguard' means open -> lifeguard, and thunderstorm -> no lifeguard. Chaining gives thunderstorm -> no lifeguard -> not open. B and C are converses. D is an inverse. E converts 'only if' into 'if'. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-wave6-tili-reading-logic-run6) reached the same answer: Open means a lifeguard is on duty, and a thunderstorm means no lifeguard. Chaining these, a thunderstorm means no lifeguard, so the lido does not open. B and C are converse errors. D is an inverse error. E treats a necessary condition as sufficient.]

review.notes: Deduction item on "only if" and the contrapositive. All eight combinations of storm, lifeguard and opening were enumerated: only the storm-implies-closed conclusion holds in every consistent world. Options were reordered after review to remove answer-position bias; ids and labels were remapped with the key.
